architecture.subtitle: The framework sequences every turn through a single speaker. Model voice, tool audio, and skill-claimed bridges never collide.

mobileSummary.title: How the pieces fit
mobileSummary.intro: On a phone the diagram below collapses to a list — the relationships are easier to read than the SVG.

rows.v: Identity + skill list, loaded at startup
Browser today · ESP32 next · phone via the PWA

turnCoord.v: Model speech always finishes before tool audio. Interrupts are atomic — drop flag, clear queue, flush, cancel.

skillDispatch.v: Python packages registered via entry-points. Typed context, namespaced storage, no framework internals leaked.

proactive.v: Skills call ctx.inject_turn() and Huxley speaks first — without waiting for the user. Timers, alerts, doorbells, inbound messages.

bridging.v: Skills can claim the mic and speaker for full-duplex audio (calls, voice memos). The focus manager prevents collisions with model speech.

constraints.v: never_say_no, confirm_destructive, child_safe — declared in persona.yaml and enforced system-wide. Build for vulnerable users without special code.

provider.v: OpenAI Realtime today; the architecture leaves room for other providers, but Huxley itself doesn’t train or serve models.

timeline.subtitle: The coordinator drains model speech before tool audio starts, holds proactive turns until the channel is free, and makes every interrupt atomic.

callouts.t2Body: Model finishes its sentence before the chime plays.
callouts.t3Body: Proactive inject waits for the previous turn to drain.

rows.v: User holds the button: "Set a timer for 25 minutes."
Tool chime plays — only after model speech drains.
Proactive inject (later): "Timer's up." Holds until the channel is free.

skills.subtitle: Skills register via Python entry-points. Add a line to persona.yaml, restart — the framework never changes.
skills.writingTitle: A skill is a Python package.
skills.writingBody: Declare tools. Handle calls. Return a ToolResult — optionally with an AudioStream, a PlaySound, or an InputClaim for full-duplex audio. The framework sequences the rest.

today.subtitle: Real numbers from the current commit. The framework is small, opinionated, and tested.
today.roadmapSubtitle: The full plan lives in docs/roadmap.md. These four are the next visible moves.

cookbook.v: A third-party author should write a working skill in under 30 minutes with no Huxley-internals knowledge.

secrets.v: ${HUXLEY_TELEGRAM_TOKEN} in persona.yaml — declare the shape of the secret without storing it. Lands before stage 4.

providerAbstraction.v: Extract OpenAI Realtime as one implementation of a VoiceProvider interface. Triggered when a credible second provider exists.

esp32.v: Replaces the browser as the main production client. Same WebSocket protocol; firmware lives at clients/firmware/.

personas.subtitle: A persona is a YAML file: voice, language, skills, guardrails. Six examples showing how far the same framework stretches.

install.cost: Runs on OpenAI Realtime: roughly $0.06/min listening, $0.24/min speaking. You pay OpenAI directly — Huxley adds no markup. Idle is free.

hx1.subtitle: HX-1 is the walkie-talkie Huxley's first persona speaks through. It was made for an elderly blind user: no screen, no wake word, one orange lever.

viewer.aria: 3D model of HX-1. Drag to turn it.
viewer.failed: The 3D model didn't load. Reload the page to try again.

inside.title: A small board, a big speaker, two cells.

parts.v: Waveshare's round board: Wi-Fi, two microphones, an audio codec, and seven RGB LEDs on its back.
Behind it, the whole closed case is its back box, about 130 cm³, so voices come out full.
Protected cells in parallel, charged over USB-C with the power switch on. The switch sits recessed in the left side so it isn't flipped by accident.
A printed lever on a printed pin presses a 12 × 12 switch through a spring, with a short, firm click.
The board's seven LEDs sit behind the clear back, ready for a status light the firmware doesn't drive yet.
The front comes off with four screws and opens like a book. Only the two halves of the back are glued.

how.title: The walkie is the ears and the voice.
how.subtitle: Everything else happens on a Huxley server: the persona, its skills, and the call to the voice model.

steps.v: Pressing the lever in opens the microphone. Your voice streams to the server over Wi-Fi while you talk.
The server runs the persona, here Abuelo, a slow, warm voice in Spanish, and its skills: audiobooks, radio, news, reminders and messages.
The reply streams back and plays as it arrives. Press the lever again to interrupt it.

made.title: Printed at home, fitted in software.
made.body1: Every printed part comes off a desktop 3D printer: a white front, a red base, a clear PETG back over the board's LEDs, a black grille and an orange lever. The case is modelled in Python with build123d.
made.body2: Before anything is printed, tests check every part against the others and against the board's own 3D model, check that each one has a way in, and check that no layer starts in mid-air. The heavy parts are held by printed features and screws, never glue.

story.aria: HX-1 in 3D, staying on screen while you scroll down the page.

dots.title: Ten dots. One word.
dots.body: They say “hola” in braille, at twice the usual size: from across the room they look like confetti, up close they say hello. Glued on through a printed stencil.

lever.title: Hold. Talk. Let go.
lever.body: It has a lever, and that is the whole interface. While you hold it, it listens; when you let go, it answers. The rest of the time, nothing listens.

inside.body: An ESP32-S3 board with Wi-Fi and two microphones, a 40 mm speaker, two 18650 cells and a 12 × 12 switch, in a printed 70 × 104 × 37 mm case that closes with four screws.
